# The Long Way Home

The city at two in the morning is a rough draft of itself. The scaffolding shows. Streets that by day are rivers of purpose become empty sentences, unfinished, and you can walk down the middle of them — actually down the middle, along the yellow line — and feel something like the freedom the road must have promised the first person who walked one.

I started walking at night years ago, not for exercise and not for any reason I could have given at the time. I'd finish work, lie down, and discover that sleep was a country I couldn't enter without a long walk first. So I went out. The first thing you learn is that the night city is not the day city with the lights off. It's a different place that happens to share an address.

The dog walkers know this. There is a loose federation of them — the sleepless, the devoted, the recently heartbroken, the shift workers — and they nod to one another across empty intersections with a familiarity that would take months to earn in daylight. Nobody asks what you're doing out. That is the courtesy of the hour. Whatever your reason, it is understood to be sufficient.

What surprised me most was the thinking. I had assumed the walks would be empty time, a holding pattern, and instead they turned out to be the opposite: the hours when my mind finally said the things it had been mouthing all day without sound. There's a well-documented science to this — the default mode network, the way attention loosens its grip when the body is occupied with something rhythmic and undemanding — but the science feels beside the point when you're the one out there. The point is that a problem you've been pushing at all day like a stuck drawer will, somewhere around the second mile, simply open. Not because you forced it. Because you stopped leaning on it.

I remember one night in particular, in a city I didn't live in, visiting for a wedding, unable to sleep in a borrowed apartment with someone else's books on the shelves. I went out at one and walked until the streets stopped making sense, which in an unfamiliar city happens quickly and completely. I was lost in the old way, the full way: no phone signal, no map in my pocket, no name for the street. And I remember standing at an intersection of two roads I had never seen, under a streetlight that buzzed like a trapped insect, and feeling — not fear exactly, and not thrill — a kind of attention I hadn't paid to anything in years. Every building was a question. Every corner required a decision. I was, for the first time in months, entirely where I was.

We have nearly finished killing that feeling. The blue dot on the map knows where we are even when we don't, and it is patient, and it is never lost. I use it like everyone else. I have no nostalgia worth taking seriously; getting lost in a strange city at night is a luxury of the young and the careless, and it has a dark twin — getting lost when you're old, or hurt, or when it's very cold. I don't want that back. What I mind is that we've collapsed the distinction between being lost and being a stranger. You can be a stranger now without ever being lost. You can visit a city and never once not know where you are, never once feel the specific humility of the person who has to ask. The asking is the thing. The asking is how a place gets under your skin — you have to admit it is bigger than your knowledge of it.

My grandfather drove trucks for forty years and navigated by paper map, by memory, by the position of the sun, and by stopping to ask. He had a mental map of the country that was annotated with decades of small corrections: the road that floods, the diner that closed, the shortcut that isn't one anymore. He never once looked at a screen to find himself. When he died we found maps in the glovebox, in the shed, under the seat — folded into softness, their creases gone to furring, like cloth. Some of them had notes in the margins. *Road works. Bad coffee. Good dog.* He had written himself onto the country and the country onto himself, and I think that's a kind of knowledge the blue dot will never give anyone, because the blue dot does the finding and leaves you nothing to do but follow.

So now, when I can, I take the long way. Not as a practice, nothing so upright — just as an occasional surrender. I leave early and go the wrong way on purpose. I turn down a street because of the light on it, or because of a smell, cut grass or rain on hot asphalt or someone frying onions, and I follow the smell as far as it goes. I let the walk be about the walk. It's remarkable how much of my life has been spent treating movement as dead time to be minimized, routes as problems to be solved, arrival as the only real event. The long way is how I remind myself that this is a choice, and that the choice has a cost, and that the cost is everything that happens between here and there.

The other night I got home around three. The streets had been empty and then, in the last block, they weren't: a delivery truck idling, a woman in scrubs smoking outside a hospital entrance, the first pale suggestion of the day in the sky behind the water tower. I stood for a minute at my own door, key in hand, not going in. The city was still a draft. Somewhere behind me a dog was being walked, and I thought I heard the other walker nod, though I didn't turn around. Then I went in, and the lock did its small work, and I slept.

**The Long Way Home**

The city at two in the morning is a rough draft of itself. The scaffolding shows. Streets that by day are rivers of purpose become empty sentences, unfinished, and you can walk down the middle of them — actually down the middle, along the yellow line — and feel something like the freedom the road must have promised the first person who walked one.

I started walking at night years ago, not for exercise and not for any reason I could have given at the time. I'd finish work, lie down, and discover that sleep was a country I couldn't enter without a long walk first. So I went out. The first thing you learn is that the night city is not the day city with the lights off. It's a different place that happens to share an address.

The dog walkers know this. There is a loose federation of them — the sleepless, the devoted, the recently heartbroken, the shift workers — and they nod to one another across empty intersections with a familiarity that would take months to earn in daylight. Nobody asks what you're doing out. That is the courtesy of the hour. Whatever your reason, it is understood to be sufficient.

What surprised me most was the thinking. I had assumed the walks would be empty time, a holding pattern, and instead they turned out to be the opposite: the hours when my mind finally said the things it had been mouthing all day without sound. There's a well-documented science to this — the default mode network, the way attention loosens its grip when the body is occupied with something rhythmic and undemanding — but the science feels beside the point when you're the one out there. The point is that a problem you've been pushing at all day like a stuck drawer will, somewhere around the second mile, simply open. Not because you forced it. Because you stopped leaning on it.

I remember one night in particular, in a city I didn't live in, visiting for a wedding, unable to sleep in a borrowed apartment with someone else's books on the shelves. I went out at one and walked until the streets stopped making sense, which in an unfamiliar city happens quickly and completely. I was lost in the old way, the full way: no phone signal, no map in my pocket, no name for the street. And I remember standing at an intersection of two roads I had never seen, under a streetlight that buzzed like a trapped insect, and feeling — not fear exactly, and not thrill — a kind of attention I hadn't paid to anything in years. Every building was a question. Every corner required a decision. I was, for the first time in months, entirely where I was.

We have nearly finished killing that feeling. The blue dot on the map knows where we are even when we don't, and it is patient, and it is never lost. I use it like everyone else. I have no nostalgia worth taking seriously; getting lost in a strange city at night is a luxury of the young and the careless, and it has a dark twin — getting lost when you're old, or hurt, or when it's very cold. I don't want that back. What I mind is that we've collapsed the distinction between being lost and being a stranger. You can be a stranger now without ever being lost. You can visit a city and never once not know where you are, never once feel the specific humility of the person who has to ask. The asking is the thing. The asking is how a place gets under your skin — you have to admit it is bigger than your knowledge of it.

My grandfather drove trucks for forty years and navigated by paper map, by memory, by the position of the sun, and by stopping to ask. He had a mental map of the country that was annotated with decades of small corrections: the road that floods, the diner that closed, the shortcut that isn't one anymore. He never once looked at a screen to find himself. When he died we found maps in the glovebox, in the shed, under the seat — folded into softness, their creases gone to furring, like cloth. Some of them had notes in the margins. *Road works. Bad coffee. Good dog.* He had written himself onto the country and the country onto himself, and I think that's a kind of knowledge the blue dot will never give anyone, because the blue dot does the finding and leaves you nothing to do but follow.

So now, when I can, I take the long way. Not as a practice, nothing so upright — just as an occasional surrender. I leave early and go the wrong way on purpose. I turn down a street because of the light on it, or because of a smell, cut grass or rain on hot asphalt or someone frying onions, and I follow the smell as far as it goes. I let the walk be about the walk. It's remarkable how much of my life has been spent treating movement as dead time to be minimized, routes as problems to be solved, arrival as the only real event. The long way is how I remind myself that this is a choice, and that the choice has a cost, and that the cost is everything that happens between here and there.

The other night I got home around three. The streets had been empty and then, in the last block, they weren't: a delivery truck idling, a woman in scrubs smoking outside a hospital entrance, the first pale suggestion of the day in the sky behind the water tower. I stood for a minute at my own door, key in hand, not going in. The city was still a draft. Somewhere behind me a dog was being walked, and I thought I heard the other walker nod, though I didn't turn around. Then I went in, and the lock did its small work, and I slept.
